title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: oil poured from a jar falls in one thread without a break, and Ramanuja says that is what knowing God looks like

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, Ramanuja read without qualities as without bad qualities: a no and a yes in one portrait. What good quality did you add after a complaint? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `A NO AND A YES.` · `TODAY: A THREAD OF OIL.`

segments.voice: Tip a jar of oil, slowly, over a bowl. It doesn't splash or scatter. It falls in one thin, glossy thread, unbroken from the lip of the jar to the bowl below. Ramanuja reaches for that thread in the opening pages of the Sri Bhashya, when he asks a plain question about the Upanishads. They promise freedom to the one who knows Brahman. Fine. But what kind of knowing? Reading a sentence and nodding? Understanding it once, on a good afternoon? His answer is the thread of oil, and today we follow it.
screen: `OIL FALLS IN ONE THREAD.` → `WHAT KIND OF KNOWING?` → `FOLLOW THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads use more than one word for this knowing. Know. Meditate. Worship. Ramanuja argues they mean the same thing, and that it isn't a one-time flash of understanding. It's meditation that keeps going, a remembering of God that doesn't break, like oil poured in a steady stream. He takes his key phrase from the Chandogya Upanishad, which says that when one's food, the things taken in, is pure, the mind becomes pure, and when the mind is pure, remembrance becomes firm, and with firm remembrance, every knot comes loose. Dhruva smriti. Firm, steady remembrance. Then he takes a step further. Remembered steadily enough, he says, it becomes so vivid that it's like seeing. And remembrance that is like seeing, and full of love, is what the Upanishads call knowing. That's bhakti. So for Ramanuja, devotion isn't a softer path beside knowledge. It's what knowledge becomes when it doesn't stop. And there's one more turn. The Katha Upanishad says the self isn't gained by teaching or cleverness, but by the one it chooses. Ramanuja asks who gets chosen, and answers: the one who has become dearest, through this unbroken loving remembrance. So knowing, loving and being chosen run together, like one thread. The Alvars sang this. Ramanuja argues it, line by line.
screen: `KNOW, MEDITATE, WORSHIP: ONE THING.` · `LIKE OIL POURED, UNBROKEN.` · `SO STEADY IT'S LIKE SEEING.` · `KNOWING THAT DOESN'T STOP IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour one thread. Sit, and let the breath settle. Choose one thing to hold in mind: a name you pray to, a face you love, or simply the breath. Let attention flow toward it slowly and evenly, like oil from a tipped jar. When it breaks, don't scold yourself. Just tip the jar again and let the thread start over. Count nothing. Only keep pouring. If you pray, you can let the thread be the name you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vaishnava theology. Today, knowing God as dhruva smriti: steady remembrance, poured like oil, so vivid it's like seeing, and full of love. Today's word.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas cultivate steady remembrance of Vishnu through daily worship, recitation of his names and of the Alvar hymns, and quiet meditation, and teachers point to Ramanuja's image of oil poured in an unbroken stream.

fork.setup: the Upanishads promise freedom to the one who knows Brahman. you're Ramanuja. what kind of knowing do you say they mean?
options: remembrance that never breaks, full of love.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads it as unbroken remembrance, like oil poured, so vivid it's like seeing: and that, he says, is bhakti.

original.note: Sanskrit: firm remembrance, from the Chandogya Upanishad, which Ramanuja reads as the knowing that frees.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowledge and devotion are two different paths.
what it means: for Ramanuja, knowing Brahman is unbroken loving remembrance, which is devotion.
what a scholar hears: Sri Bhashya on 1.1.1: vedana as upasana, dhruva smriti from Chandogya 7.26.2, the oil-stream image, and Katha 1.2.23's 'whom it chooses' read as the dearest.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya 1.1.1 (knowing as meditation; steady remembrance like oil poured; like seeing; bhakti)
Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2 (pure food, pure mind, firm remembrance, knots loosened)
Katha Upanishad 1.2.23 (not gained by teaching or intellect; gained by the one it chooses)

notes: The oil-stream image (tailadharavat) and 'like seeing' (darshana-samanakara) are from the Sri Bhashya's long comment on 1.1.1; confirm the paraphrase.
Chandogya 7.26.2 is paraphrased (ahara-shuddhi: 'food' read as what is taken in); confirm.
Ramanuja's reading of Katha 1.2.23 ('the one it chooses' as the one who is dearest) is paraphrased; confirm. Day 249 told the Katha line without this reading.
Day 465 (Yoga Sutras) used an 'unbroken flow' for dhyana; this day's image is Ramanuja's own, but an editor may want to check the overlap.
Devanagari ध्रुवा स्मृतिः and the stress in 'say' should be checked.
Editor: the hook's claim that water breaks into drops where oil doesn't was cut, and the oil now pours into a bowl rather than over a lamp, since lamps carry days 1223, 1229 and 1230.
